To limit the number of relations audit logged for `SELECT` and `DML` statements, consider using object audit logging (see Object Auditing). Object audit logging allows selection of the relations to be logged allowing for reduction of the overall log volume. However, when new relations are added they must be explicitly added to object audit logging. A programmatic solution where specified tables are excluded from logging and all others are included may be a good option in this case.

Object-level audit logging is implemented via the roles system. The pgaudit.role setting defines the role that will be used for audit logging. A relation (`TABLE`, `VIEW`, etc.) will be audit logged when the audit role has permissions for the command executed or inherits the permissions from another role. This allows you to effectively have multiple audit roles even though there is a single master role in any context.

Bindery holds API keys, reaches services on your network and writes to your disks, so it is built and checked with that in mind. Every push and a weekly run go through govulncheck, CodeQL, Semgrep, gitleaks, Hadolint, Checkov, Grype, Syft, a ZAP baseline and OpenSSF Scorecard, with gosec enforced in the blocking lint gate. Release binaries and the container image carry SLSA build provenance, which you can check with `gh attestation verify` (how), and binaries ship with SBOMs. In the app: guards against server side request forgery on outbound URLs, strict response headers, and a distroless non root image with digest pinned bases. The Helm chart adds a read only root filesystem with every capability dropped.
To report a vulnerability, follow **SECURITY.md**. Published advisories are on the Security tab.

Bindery sends one anonymous ping a day to api.getbindery.dev so the maintainer can count active installs and spot widespread breakage, and the reply tells the app when a newer release exists. It carries a random install ID, the version, OS, architecture and deploy method, counts of which features are configured, and the number and fixed text of the most frequent error log lines. Never titles, paths, URLs, usernames, hostnames or IP addresses. Turn it off with `telemetry.enabled: false` in **Settings, Logs**, or `BINDERY_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true` before the first run; the update notice goes with it. Retention and deletion are in **PRIVACY.md**.

在单片机日常开发中，总会需要存储一些信息，这时就需要使用单片机FLASH存储的方案，目前单片机存储的方案有很多，比如：EASYFLASH、FLASHDB、OSAL_NV等等方案，他们程序都非常大，在存储不多的变量时不值得。而且很少有考虑到flash写入出错的情况。
在实际产品中，嵌入式产品flash写入可能会受各种因素影响（电池供电、意外断电、气温等）从而并不是很稳定，一旦出现错误，会导致产品一系列问题。
不同于其他很多的KV型数据库，TinyFlashDB每一个需要存储的变量都会分配一个单独的单片机flash扇区，变量长度不可变。
所以TinyFlashDB仅适用于存储几个关键性变量（例如：IAP跳转标志、系统断电时间等等），不适合大规模数据存储（大规模数据存储可使用EASYFLASH等）。
TinyFlashDB在设计时就考虑了写入错误的影响，追求力所能及的安全保障、资源占用方面尽可能的缩小（单块模式代码占用不到1kb）、尽可能的通用性（可以移植到51等8位机，无法逆序写入的stm32L4系列，某些flash加密的单片机和其他普通32位机上）。

每次写入后都会再读取出来进行校验，如果校验不通过，就会继续在下一个地址继续尝试写入。直到达到最大写入次数（TFDB_WRITE_MAX_RETRY）或者头部校验错误。
读取数据时也会计算和校验，不通过的话继续读取，直到返回校验通过的最新数据，或者读取失败。
数据前部两字节seq的合法值由`TFDB_DUAL_SEQ_COUNT`决定：默认为3种（0x00ff->0x0ff0->0xff00），可配置为5种（0xff00->0xf0f0->0x0ff0->0x0f0f->0x00ff）。
如此循环往复，通过读取两个block中最新变量的seq来判断哪个flash扇区中存储的是最新值。
当最新值存储在第一扇区时，下次写入则会在第二扇区写入，反之亦然。
5值循环将`tfdb_dual_get_pre`的判别窗口从3次写入扩大到5次写入，两块中需要更多条连续损坏记录才会出现判别歧义；两套值集互不兼容，且切换无法被程序检测——部分旧值在另一套循环中仍是合法值，不重新初始化直接切换会使库静默误判最新数据所在的扇区（返回旧数据），所以切换配置前必须擦除并重新初始化两个flash块。
`tfdb_dual_get_pre`通过seq在循环中的前后关系，比较两个候选记录（另一扇区中最新的记录，和当前扇区中的上一条有效记录）哪个是上一次保存的数据，即使其中一条候选记录损坏，也能返回可以读取到的最新的较早数据。

Target system architecture. Execution cells send Actions to the enforcement node, which holds the gateways, the sandbox supervisor, the egress proxy, the enforcement kernel, the evidence writer and the control agent. The egress proxy is the only path to the untrusted world. Execution lifecycle: no effect before a durable decision

The twelve-step lifecycle: propose, normalise, admit, authorize, evaluate state, consult advisors, combine, approve when required, record, execute, observe and verify, inspect and deliver. Failures end in one of four outcomes: refused and recorded; no grant and cell paused; killed and session halted; or result withheld.
Information flow: typed, labelled values only

Untrusted content and secret data go to a quarantined worker with no effect tools. It returns a typed value, whose schema and size are checked, to the planner context. Every effect the planner proposes passes a flow check before reaching egress destinations, tools with effects or other agents.
Emergency governance: one person stops, two people resume

Control states: running, suspended, locked down, stopped and recovering. One person can stop from any of the first three. Resuming, lifting a lockdown and leaving stopped each take two people, and recovering returns to running once checks pass.

The distributed base drops every reducible subsystem (both interpreters, the HTTP core + web bindings, the Keel event loop + server, mbedTLS + TLS transport, SQLite, WASM/WAMR, image codecs) and `hull build` composes back exactly what the app uses via signed feature archives whole-archived in at link time. Hull is at **v0.18.0** (2026-11-03). Pre-stable: APIs and the manifest schema may change. Pin versions and read the changelog before upgrading. v0.18.0 carries security audit rounds 18-43 and the audit-convergence campaign: measured-time charging and request deadlines, connection and request concurrency caps, refused session-altering SQL, Hull's internal tables in a database file it owns (moved automatically on first start, with a one-release rollback flag), and build-time-only GPU shaders. Several defaults changed (10 s request deadline, per-client connection limits, header and keep-alive deadlines, `remote_addr` on dual-stack listeners), so read the upgrade notes before moving. v0.17.1 carries security audit round 17: Postgres / MySQL replies and connection startup, Valkey scans, GPU memory and tar parsing are now charged or bounded, a built binary no longer reads templates or modules from disk beside it, and tool spawns never run a program from the working directory. Tool bundles installed by an earlier release (`zig`, the musl floors) must be reinstalled once. The v0.17.0 release carries security audit rounds 14, 15 and 16 and Keel v3.3.1 (SSE events written as one batched chunk). Some calls that used to pass silently now raise, refuse or rate-limit - non-positive or string ttls, over-heap `fs.read` / `blob.get` / `db.async` results, persistent WASM instances growing past their heap, an unrate-limited email-change mail - so read the release's upgrade notes before moving. It also fixes the Windows source build. Earlier: v0.15.0 completed the first-party Windows install story and widened backend + test coverage: `install.ps1` ships with non-admin installer tests plus Winget and Scoop metadata, the cosmo base compiles in the PostgreSQL and MySQL wire backends, `hull tools install` gains `--tag=` to pull from a named release, and SMTP now routes through Keel v3 public primitives. Two capability-layer fixes land with it: a server-supplied SCRAM iteration count is now bounded (an unbounded one let a hostile or MITM'd PostgreSQL server stall the client in PBKDF2), and `hull/search` rejects a SQL keyword as an identifier on the JS side as it already did on the Lua side. The 28 co-located stdlib test suites under `stdlib/{lua,js}/hull/tests/` now run in CI for the first time; wiring them up also surfaced an uninitialised read in vendored QuickJS that every `const [a, b] = x` triggered (see `docs/quickjs_patches.md`). **Windows note (v0.15.0):** Hull process startup on Windows was measured at about 53ms slower per invocation than v0.14.0, traced to the vendored Keel v3.1.1 bump and reported upstream; it is felt most by tooling that shells out repeatedly. **Windows upgrade note:** a v0.13.0 Windows binary cannot self-update (that fix ships in v0.14.0); download `hull-cosmo` and replace `hull` once manually while it is not running, after which `hull update` works normally. **Rolling Memory** is a source-available, local-first memory tool for AI coding agents — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, ZCode, and more — built on the **Rolling Autonoetic Memory Engine**. It indexes supported conversation sources and mounted files locally for connected agents to query through one MCP tool: `recall`. See the integration guide for collection limits and manual import. **No cloud required, no vectors, no background LLM calls**; free for every noncommercial use.

> **Get started**: Run `curl -fsSL https://github.com/rocareer/rolling-memory/raw/main/install.sh | bash` (or `bash install.sh` from a local checkout) to wire your coding assistants, then just chat normally. Whenever you need to trace back history, ask something like *"Where did we fix that bug last time?"* See the Quick Start Guide for details.

- **Safe and private (no third party in the middle)**: Everything compiles to a single zero-dependency Go binary (`CGO_ENABLED=0`) and lives in one SQLite file on your machine, with zero network requests in the memory layer — **other than you and the agent actively working for you, no third-party memory service, embedding provider, or external server ever sees your code, file paths, or conversations.** One precise boundary: if your coding agent uses a remote LLM API, the passages `recall` returns travel to that model provider as part of your prompt (see docs/privacy.md §1);

- **Built-in USB portable mode**: Because both the binary and the SQLite vault are self-contained files, we also included a USB portable mode (see `docs/usb-portable.md`) so you can put the tool and your memory vault onto a thumb drive and carry them around. It is still experimental and not thoroughly tested yet, and it comes with a real prerequisite: **for project-specific memories to be useful on another machine, you have to be working on the same project there**. If you are curious and like tinkering, feel free to try it out and tell us what works and what does not.

> **About this release**: This repository ships **pure local mode (`local_plain`)**: recall, storage, and consolidation all run in the local vault, with no memory-plane network requests. The only outbound calls are the evaluation LLM endpoint you configure, the optional upstream benchmark-corpus download, and the optional update check. A separate **cloud memory service** — ciphertext-only by design and aimed at advanced and enterprise users — is offered by application and is not part of this repository; see DECLARATION.md for the release and license boundary and SUPPORT.md for how to get help.

Connected tools can query the same local SQLite vault, including records imported from supported sources. Connecting a tool does not itself import that tool's conversation history.
Model-written summaries can contain mistakes. For imported records, `recall` can return source passages and provenance for you and your agent to check.

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_YYJSON`|`OFF`|Enable the **yyjson JSON backend** (`src/yyjson/`) — the library's **own bundled** parser alongside nlohmann, with the same accessor names (`uvcpp_json_get_string/bool/int/double`) and the same statuses — **both directions of JSON come out of that one production library**: `uvcpp_json_doc` / `uvcpp_json_value` parse, and `uvcpp_json_builder` / `uvcpp_json_node` construct a tree that `uvcpp_json_write` serialises with **yyjson's own writer** (no hand-rolled serializer on this path; the old bridge into `uvcpp_json_writer` was removed in 1.7.2). Its parse is faster, its DOM is smaller, and nothing on the path recurses — not the parser, not the writer. **Turned off, nothing about the nlohmann path changes** (`using uvcpp_json = nlohmann::json` and every `uvcpp_json_*` keep their behaviour; the exported symbol set and `DT_NEEDED` of the library are unchanged). yyjson is a **private** dependency (one header + one `.c`, compiled as object code into the same `uvcpp` library — no extra artifact), fetched via `FetchContent`. **As of 1.7.0 it is in the release package** — all six release legs enable it (earlier packages did not), and four CI jobs really build it: the Ubuntu / macOS / MSVC matrix entries plus the single `ci-mingw64.yml` job. See `doc/json-guide.md` §13|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_BROTLI`|`OFF`|Enable the **brotli body compressor** — `br` as a second `Content-Encoding` for HTTP response bodies next to gzip/deflate, picked by the same `Accept-Encoding` negotiation (`br` wins on `q`-ties with gzip because it is the smaller of the two; `*` and the zlib-less build are covered too). **What it buys is bytes on the wire, not speed**: at the default quality the same body is ~11 % smaller than gzip level 6, and because the compressed variant is served out of the response cache the per-request cost is the same as gzip's — an entry that compresses without a cache tag pays for the encode every request. The default quality is `5` (brotli's own default), deliberately not `0`. **Turned off, nothing changes** (no `br` in `Accept-Encoding` negotiation, and the exported symbol set / `DT_NEEDED` of the library are unchanged). brotli is a **private** dependency, found via pkg-config/`find_library` when the system has it and built from source via `FetchContent` (tag pinned to `BROTLI_VERSION`) otherwise — **two** static libraries, so a static-library user links `-lbrotlienc -lbrotlidec` themselves. **As of 1.7.0 it is in the release package** — every release leg passes `UVCPP_BROTLI_FROM_SOURCE=ON` so the package stays self-contained — and five CI jobs really build it: the Ubuntu `brotli` + `brotli-no-zlib`, macOS and MSVC matrix entries plus the single `ci-mingw64.yml` job. See `doc/web-http-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_BROTLI_FROM_SOURCE`|`OFF`|Skip the system lookup entirely (`find_package(PkgConfig)` → `find_path`/`find_library`) and build brotli from the source pinned by `BROTLI_VERSION`, linking it statically. **The lookup runs system-first**, so on a machine that happens to have `libbrotli-dev` the "links the static `.a`" promise silently turns into three `DT_NEEDED` entries (`libbrotlienc` / `libbrotlidec` / `libbrotlicommon`) — and nothing turns red, because the release workflow's `ldd` blacklist does not name brotli. Any release leg that enables brotli passes this so its package stays self-contained. The discovery block is skipped *without being called* (its results land in the CMake cache, so calling it once would leak the previous answer into the next configure of the same tree). Default `OFF` leaves today's behaviour byte-for-byte. See `doc/web-http-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_CAPI`|`OFF`|Export the **C ABI** (`src/capi/`, C99 headers for C#/P-Invoke and any other FFI) out of the same `uvcpp` library — no extra artifact. Requires `UVCPP_BUILD_NET=ON` and `UVCPP_BUILD_WEB=ON`; force-disabled without them (the C surface spans net/web/webapp). **Turned on for every release configuration.** See `doc/capi-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB`|`OFF`|Enable the **database module** (`src/db/`): one `uvcpp_db_client` per connection over SQLite / MySQL / PostgreSQL / ODBC, with table-style access to the result rows. It is the only module that **requires a third-party client library** (libsqlite3 / libmysqlclient / libpq / an ODBC driver manager) — force-disabled only when those four SQL back-ends and the MongoDB one below are all missing. **Every release configuration turns it on, with all three client-library backends**: SQLite is compiled in from source, and MySQL/PostgreSQL are in the package but loaded at run time (next rows); whether the ODBC backend is in a given package depends on whether that build machine had `sql.h` (next-next row). The module also carries a MongoDB client (the row after ODBC), which is **not** part of this back-end list. See `doc/db-guide.md`|
|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB_SQLITE`|`ON`|Build the SQLite backend of the db module (needs `sqlite3.h` + libsqlite3). Not found ⇒ **this one backend is force-disabled with a warning**; the others still build|

|`UVCPP_DB_SQLITE_FROM_SOURCE`|`OFF`|Build that SQLite backend from a **hash-pinned source amalgamation** (one static `sqlite3.c`, forced PIC) instead of `find_package(SQLite3)`. **The six release legs use it**: linking the system `libsqlite3.so` would add a `DT_NEEDED` and break the packages' self-contained promise, while the system `libsqlite3.a` on Ubuntu 24.04 is not PIC (verified: `R_X86_64_PC32 … can not be used when making a shared object`). Needs network at configure time, or the zip placed by hand; both are described in `doc/db-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB_MYSQL`|`ON`|Build the MySQL backend (needs `mysql.h` + libmysqlclient). Non-standard installs: `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=…` or `-DUVCPP_DB_MYSQL_INCLUDE_DIR=… -DUVCPP_DB_MYSQL_LIBRARY=…`. **On by default, and on in every release package** (with `UVCPP_DB_RUNTIME_LOAD=ON`, which is what keeps the package loadable without libmysqlclient)|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB_PGSQL`|`ON`|Build the PostgreSQL backend (needs `libpq-fe.h` + libpq). Non-standard installs: `-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=…` or `-DPostgreSQL_INCLUDE_DIR=… -DPostgreSQL_LIBRARY=…`. **On by default, and on in every release package** (with `UVCPP_DB_RUNTIME_LOAD=ON`)|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB_ODBC`|`ON`|Build the ODBC backend of the db module (needs `sql.h` + a driver manager: `libodbc` on Linux, the system `odbc32` on Windows). Unlike the three above, it targets **an interface, not one database** — *what* it connects to is chosen by the connection string's `Driver=` / `DSN=` (Microsoft ships no linkable C client library for SQL Server; `msodbcsql18` *is* an ODBC driver), and it tries no other driver name. Not found ⇒ **this one backend is force-disabled with a warning**; the others still build. It honours `UVCPP_DB_RUNTIME_LOAD` like MySQL/PG: what gets linked is the **driver manager**, which is a client library of the same kind (a plain unixODBC package on Linux/macOS; on Windows `odbc32.dll` belongs to the OS, so linking it costs nothing). So "is this backend built" and "is there a driver for the data source you open" are two different questions — the second is answered at `open()`, in the driver manager's own words|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_DB_MONGODB`|`ON`|Build the **MongoDB backend** (`<db/uvcpp_mongo.h>`, class `uvcpp_mongo_client`): JSON in, JSON out, a sync core plus async over the libuv thread pool. It is **not** an `uvcpp_db_client` back-end — `uvcpp_db_drivers()` does not list it. Only the headers (`mongoc/mongoc.h`, `bson/bson.h`) are needed at build time: `libmongoc-1.0` / `libbson-1.0` are never linked or shipped and are loaded at run time instead (`UVCPP_DB_MONGOC_LIBRARY` / `UVCPP_DB_BSON_LIBRARY` override the search); if they are missing, `open()` returns `NO_DRIVER` and the process carries on. Not found ⇒ **this backend is force-disabled with a warning**. See `doc/mongodb-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_DB_RUNTIME_LOAD`|`OFF`|Take the MySQL / PostgreSQL / ODBC / MongoDB symbols from a client library loaded **at run time** (`dlopen` / `LoadLibrary`) instead of linking it; for ODBC that library is the **driver manager** (the actual driver is still loaded by the manager itself). **The six release legs use it, and the reason is the packages' users, not the library**: `DT_NEEDED` (the PE import table on Windows) is resolved at **load time**, so linking libmysqlclient/libpq/libodbc means a machine that has never installed those libraries cannot even *load* the library — even if it only ever runs HTTP and never touches `db`. With this on, such a machine runs everything except "actually connecting to MySQL/PG/ODBC", where it gets `uvcpp_db_status::NO_DRIVER` plus a message naming the candidates that were tried (`UVCPP_DB_MYSQL_LIBRARY` / `UVCPP_DB_PGSQL_LIBRARY` / `UVCPP_DB_ODBC_LIBRARY` / `UVCPP_DB_MONGOC_LIBRARY` / `UVCPP_DB_BSON_LIBRARY` override the search). It changes only *where the symbols come from*, not *which backends exist*: `mysql.h` / `libpq-fe.h` / `sql.h` are still needed at configure time (`MYSQL_BIND`'s layout has to come from the real header), so `UVCPP_DB_MYSQL_ENABLE` / `UVCPP_DB_PGSQL_ENABLE` / `UVCPP_DB_ODBC_ENABLE` still mean "the header was found". Default `OFF` leaves today's behaviour byte-for-byte. See `doc/db-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_REDIS`|`ON`|Enable the **Redis client** (`src/redis/`): built-in RESP2/RESP3, asynchronous over `uvcpp_tcp_client`, with AUTH / SELECT / pipelines / pub-sub / `HELLO 3` / `rediss://`. **No third-party client library is needed** (not hiredis), which is why it is on by default; it depends on the net module and is force-disabled when `UVCPP_BUILD_NET=OFF`. See `doc/redis-guide.md`|
|`UVCPP_BUILD_LIBUV_FROM_SOURCE`|`OFF`|Fetch and build libuv from source via `FetchContent`|

|`UVCPP_STATIC_RUNTIME`|`OFF`|Statically link the compiler runtime (`libgcc`/`libstdc++`) into the library. **MinGW and Linux only — a no-op on MSVC**, which uses `/MD` and ships `vcruntime`/`msvcp` in the package. **On Linux it also applies to every executable, and a *shared* `libuvcpp.so` built with it cannot be combined with a consumer that uses the system `libstdc++.so.6`** — both copies instantiate the same COMDAT templates (`std::once_flag`'s `__once_proxy`, `std::__future_base::_State_baseV2`) and ELF's global symbol scope makes one side jump into the other's frame, so the failure is a run-time segfault or `double free`, **not a link error**. **That is why the release workflow's two Linux legs no longer pass it** (1.7.0 onwards) — the Linux packages therefore need the system `libstdc++.so.6` / `libgcc_s.so.1`, which every distro with a C++ runtime already has. The two MinGW legs still pass it: PE has no global symbol scope, so there is nothing to interpose, and a MinGW user's machine may not have `libstdc++-6.dll`. See `doc/build-guide.md`|
|`UVCPP_ENABLE_TRY_WRITE`|`ON`|Try `uv_try_write` before copying into a write buffer|
|`UVCPP_TRY_WRITE_MIN_BYTES`|`32768`|Smallest payload worth attempting `uv_try_write` for (a `CACHE STRING`, not an `option()`)|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_UDP_GSO`|`ON` when Windows **and** `UVCPP_ENABLE_QUIC=ON`, else `OFF`|Send-side UDP Segmentation Offload for the QUIC transport: hand a batch of equal-sized datagrams to the stack in **one** `WSASendTo` via `UDP_SEND_MSG_SIZE`, instead of one syscall per datagram. The segment size is taken from what each aggregate write reports, so the wire carries exactly the datagrams it carries today. **Windows only** — the code is compiled out elsewhere and the switch is a no-op there. See `doc/quic-guide.md`|
